lessons.title: Testing Water Parameters: pH, DO, Ammonia
lessons.body: Water quality is the foundation of fish health. You must test regularly. For pH, use a liquid test kit or electronic meter. Ideal range for tilapia and catfish is 6.5 to 8.5. Test at least twice a week, early morning. If pH is below 6.5, add agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) at 100-200 kg per hectare. If above 8.5, add gypsum or partially exchange water. Dissolved oxygen (DO) is critical. Fish need at least 4 mg/L; below 2 mg/L they gasp at surface. Use a DO meter or chemical test kit. Test at dawn when DO is lowest. If low, increase aeration by splashing water or using a paddle wheel aerator. Ammonia is toxic. Unionized ammonia (NH3) is deadly above 0.1 mg/L. Test with a kit. Ammonia comes from fish waste and uneaten feed. To reduce, stop feeding for a day, increase aeration, and do a 30% water exchange. In Africa, many farmers use simple tools: a secchi disk for clarity, a thermometer, and locally made test kits from agricultural suppliers. Record all readings in a notebook. Always test before and after adding any treatment. Remember, consistent monitoring prevents fish kills. Start with a basic kit: pH, ammonia, and DO. These three tests will save your fish.

lessons.title: Water Treatment: Chlorination and Dechlorination
lessons.body: Chlorine is used to disinfect water, killing bacteria and viruses. But chlorine is also toxic to fish. You must dechlorinate before adding water to your pond. For chlorination, use calcium hypochlorite (bleaching powder) at 5-10 mg/L for empty ponds. For water supply, if using municipal water, it may already contain chlorine. Test with a chlorine test kit. To dechlorinate, you can use sodium thiosulfate. Dose: 1 gram per 100 liters of water to neutralize 1 mg/L chlorine. Alternatively, let water sit in an open tank for 24-48 hours in sunlight; chlorine evaporates. In rural Africa, many farmers use rainwater or well water, which may not need chlorination. But if you must treat, always dechlorinate. For emergency fish health, potassium permanganate at 2-4 mg/L can treat external parasites, but it also kills beneficial bacteria. Use only in isolated tanks. Never chlorinate a pond with fish. If you accidentally add chlorine, immediately add sodium thiosulfate or do a large water exchange. Store chemicals in a dry, dark place. Wear gloves and goggles. Measure carefully; overdose can kill everything. After dechlorination, test again to confirm zero chlorine. Then add water to pond. Always have a backup water source. In Africa, sun-drying water in black tanks is a cheap dechlorination method. Remember: chlorine kills fish, so treat with respect.

lessons.title: Biological Filtration and Nitrification
lessons.body: Biological filtration uses beneficial bacteria to convert toxic ammonia into less harmful nitrate. This process is called nitrification. Two types of bacteria do the work: Nitrosomonas convert ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter convert nitrite to nitrate. Nitrate is safe up to 200 mg/L for most fish. To grow these bacteria, you need a biofilter with high surface area. Common materials: plastic bioballs, lava rock, or even cut plastic bottles. Water must flow over the media. In Africa, many farmers build trickle filters using buckets filled with gravel and sand. The bacteria colonize within 4-6 weeks. Start by adding a source of ammonia (fish waste or ammonium chloride) to feed them. Keep pH between 7 and 8, temperature 25-30Â°C. Avoid chlorinated water; it kills bacteria. If you use chlorinated water, dechlorinate first. Test for ammonia and nitrite daily during startup. When both read zero, your filter is cycled. Then you can add fish gradually. For maintenance, rinse filter media in pond water, never tap water. If ammonia spikes, do a 50% water exchange and add a bacterial starter culture. Commercial starters are available, but you can also use mud from a healthy pond. In a well-cycled pond, nitrification happens naturally in the pond bottom and on walls. But a dedicated biofilter allows higher stocking densities. Always have backup aeration. Nitrification consumes oxygen, so DO must be above 4 mg/L. Monitor nitrite; it is toxic above 0.5 mg/L. With proper filtration, your fish will thrive.

lessons.title: Managing Algae and Aquatic Plants
lessons.body: Algae are microscopic plants that turn water green. A little algae is goodâit produces oxygen and feeds fish. But too much causes problems: low oxygen at night, clogged filters, and off-flavor in fish. To control algae, reduce nutrients. Don't overfeed; uneaten feed fuels algae. Maintain a healthy plant cover: floating plants like water hyacinth or water lettuce shade the pond and absorb nutrients. But be carefulâwater hyacinth can become invasive. Use 10-20% coverage. For string algae, manually remove with a rake. For planktonic algae (green water), use barley straw: place 50 g per square meter in a mesh bag. As it decomposes, it releases compounds that inhibit algae. In Africa, many farmers use tilapia to control algaeâthey graze on it. Stock 2-3 tilapia per square meter. For serious blooms, use copper sulfate at 0.5 mg/L, but this is toxic to fish at higher doses and kills invertebrates. Better to use aeration and water exchange. Aquatic plants like water lilies provide shade and habitat, but they can cover the pond. Limit to 25% coverage. Remove dead plants to prevent oxygen depletion. If you see blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), it's toxic. Do not let fish eat it. Treat with a 30% water exchange and add aeration. Test for ammonia and nitriteâhigh nutrients cause blooms. In summary, balance is key: some algae and plants are beneficial, but too much is harmful. Monitor weekly and act early.

lessons.title: Emergency Water Quality Interventions
lessons.body: Emergencies happen: sudden fish kills, gasping, or erratic swimming. Act fast. First, identify the problem. Test pH, ammonia, nitrite, and DO immediately. If fish gasp at surface, DO is low. Turn on all aerators, splash water, or add fresh water. If ammonia is high, do a 50% water exchange with dechlorinated water. Stop feeding for 24-48 hours. Add zeolite or activated carbon to absorb ammonia. If pH is crash (below 5), add agricultural lime at 200 kg/ha. If pH is too high (above 9), add gypsum or do a water exchange. For chlorine emergency, add sodium thiosulfate at 1 g per 100 L. For nitrite spike, add salt (sodium chloride) at 0.1% (1 kg per 1000 L) to block nitrite toxicity. Always have emergency supplies: dechlorinator, lime, salt, and a backup pump. In Africa, power cuts are common. Use a generator or manual paddle wheel. If you have no electricity, use a bucket to splash water for hours. For fish kills, remove dead fish immediately to prevent ammonia spike. Do not feed until water quality is stable. After the crisis, review your monitoring records to prevent recurrence. Keep a emergency contact for local extension officer. Remember, quick action saves fish. Never add chemicals without testing first. In an emergency, water exchange is your best friend. Have a reserve tank of dechlorinated water ready. Train your workers on emergency procedures. A calm, systematic response is key.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Monitoring Systems
lessons.body: Record keeping is not paperworkâit's your early warning system. Keep a logbook for each pond. Record daily: water temperature (morning and evening), pH, DO, ammonia, nitrite, and fish behavior. Also record feeding amounts, fish deaths, and treatments. Use a simple notebook or a whiteboard near the pond. In Africa, many farmers use a calendar to mark testing days. Test at least twice a week for pH and ammonia, daily for DO in intensive systems. For DO, test at dawn. For pH, test at 6 AM and 2 PM. Write down everything. After a month, you'll see patterns: when ammonia rises, when algae blooms. This helps you predict problems. For example, if pH drops every morning, you know to add lime. If ammonia spikes after feeding, reduce feed. Share records with your extension officer. Use a smartphone to take photos of test results. Create a simple graph: plot ammonia over time. If it trends up, act. For monitoring systems, you can install a floating thermometer and a secchi disk. For DO, a battery-powered meter is best. In remote areas, use a chemical test kit. Always calibrate meters. Store kits in a cool, dry place. At the end of each month, review your records. Calculate average pH and ammonia. Set targets: pH 7-8, ammonia <0.1 mg/L. If off, adjust. Keep records for at least one year. This data helps you improve. Remember, what gets measured gets managed. Good records lead to healthy fish and higher profits.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH range for tilapia and catfish?
quiz.explanation: Tilapia and catfish thrive in slightly acidic to slightly alkaline water, with 6.5-8.5 being optimal.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to measure dissolved oxygen?
quiz.explanation: A DO meter specifically measures dissolved oxygen in water.

quiz.q: At what ammonia level is unionized ammonia deadly to fish?
quiz.explanation: Unionized ammonia is highly toxic, and levels above 0.1 mg/L can kill fish.

quiz.q: What is the first action if fish are gasping at the surface?
quiz.explanation: Gasping indicates low dissolved oxygen, so increasing aeration is the immediate response.

quiz.q: How often should you test pH and ammonia in a pond?
options: B) At least twice a week
quiz.explanation: Regular testing at least twice a week helps catch problems early.

quiz.q: What chemical is used to dechlorinate water?
quiz.explanation: Sodium thiosulfate neutralizes chlorine quickly and safely.

quiz.q: How much sodium thiosulfate is needed to neutralize 1 mg/L chlorine in 100 liters?
quiz.explanation: The standard dose is 1 gram per 100 liters for 1 mg/L chlorine.

quiz.q: What is a cheap dechlorination method in rural Africa?
options: B) Sun-drying water in black tanks
quiz.explanation: Sunlight and open air allow chlorine to evaporate naturally.

quiz.q: What happens if you add chlorinated water directly to a fish pond?
quiz.explanation: Chlorine is toxic to fish and can cause mass mortality.

quiz.q: Which chemical can treat external parasites but also kills beneficial bacteria?
quiz.explanation: Potassium permanganate is an oxidizer that kills parasites but also harms nitrifying bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the process of converting ammonia to nitrate called?
quiz.explanation: Nitrification is the biological oxidation of ammonia to nitrite then nitrate.

quiz.q: Which bacteria convert ammonia to nitrite?
quiz.explanation: Nitrosomonas is the genus responsible for ammonia oxidation.

quiz.q: How long does it take for a biofilter to cycle?
quiz.explanation: Beneficial bacteria need 4-6 weeks to colonize and establish a functioning biofilter.

quiz.q: What should you never use to rinse biofilter media?
quiz.explanation: Tap water contains chlorine that kills beneficial bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the safe upper limit for nitrate in most fish ponds?
quiz.explanation: Nitrate is relatively safe up to 200 mg/L for most fish.

quiz.q: Which floating plant can help control algae but may become invasive?
quiz.explanation: Water hyacinth absorbs nutrients but can spread rapidly and block waterways.

quiz.q: What is the recommended coverage of floating plants in a pond?
quiz.explanation: 10-20% coverage provides shade and nutrient uptake without depleting oxygen.

quiz.q: What is a natural method to control algae using barley straw?
options: A) Add 50 g per square meter
B) Add 500 g per square meter
C) Add 5 kg per square meter
quiz.explanation: Barley straw at 50 g/mÂ² releases compounds that inhibit algae growth.

quiz.q: Which fish is commonly used to control algae in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Tilapia graze on algae and help keep ponds clean.

quiz.q: What is the danger of blue-green algae (cyanobacteria)?
options: A) It is toxic to fish
quiz.explanation: Cyanobacteria can produce toxins that kill fish and harm livestock.

quiz.q: What is the first step in an emergency water quality problem?
quiz.explanation: Testing identifies the specific problem so you can treat it correctly.

quiz.q: What should you do if ammonia is high?
quiz.explanation: Water exchange dilutes ammonia and is the fastest emergency response.

quiz.q: How much salt is used to treat nitrite toxicity?
quiz.explanation: A 0.1% salt solution blocks nitrite uptake by fish gills.

quiz.q: What is a good emergency backup for aeration during power cuts?
quiz.explanation: Manual paddling or splashing water increases oxygen without electricity.

quiz.q: Why should you remove dead fish immediately?
quiz.explanation: Decomposing fish release ammonia, worsening water quality.

quiz.q: What should be recorded daily in a pond logbook?
quiz.explanation: A complete record includes all these parameters to track pond health.

quiz.q: When is the best time to test dissolved oxygen?
quiz.explanation: DO is lowest at dawn after a night of respiration without photosynthesis.

quiz.q: What is the target ammonia level in a healthy pond?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia should be kept below 0.1 mg/L to avoid toxicity.

quiz.q: How long should you keep pond records?
quiz.explanation: Keeping at least one year of records helps identify seasonal patterns.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to measure water clarity?
quiz.explanation: A Secchi disk measures transparency, indicating algae density.
